title: 1 Samuel 30:7–20
context: David asks Abiathar for the ephod and inquires of the LORD, who tells him to pursue and promises full recovery. Pressing on with four hundred men while two hundred stay exhausted at the brook Besor, David’s men find an abandoned Egyptian servant, revive him with food, and follow his guidance to the celebrating raiders, whom David defeats, recovering everything and everyone. Both traditions read this as shared ground on seeking God’s guidance, kindness to a stranger, and God’s faithfulness to his word.

verses.text: David said to Abiathar the priest, the son of Ahimelech, “Please bring the ephod here to me.” Abiathar brought the ephod to David.
verses.arminianNotes:
David asks Abiathar the priest to bring the ephod. Arminian readers note that David’s first action after strengthening himself in God is to seek God’s guidance.

Abiathar had come to David with the ephod after the massacre at Nob (1 Sam 22:20–23; 23:6).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the contrast with Saul, who received no answer from the LORD (1 Sam 28:6).

David seeks God’s will through the means God provided, which both traditions see as a mark of his dependence on the LORD.

verses.text: David inquired of the LORD, saying, “If I pursue after this troop, will I overtake them?” He answered him, “Pursue, for you will surely overtake them, and will without fail recover all.”
verses.arminianNotes:
David asks whether he will overtake the troop, and the LORD answers, “Pursue, for you will surely overtake them, and will without fail recover all.” Arminian readers note God’s gracious answer to David’s request.

The promise is specific and complete.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see God’s word going before David’s action. The outcome is promised before the pursuit begins.

Both traditions agree that God’s guidance invites obedient action, and that David must still go and fight.

verses.text: So David went, he and the six hundred men who were with him, and came to the brook Besor, where those who were left behind stayed.
verses.arminianNotes:
David sets out with six hundred men and reaches the brook Besor, where some are left behind. Arminian readers note the cost of the pursuit for men already weary from travel.

The brook’s location is uncertain.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see David acting promptly on God’s word.

The mention of those left behind prepares for the dispute over the plunder in verses 21–25.

verses.text: But David pursued, he and four hundred men; for two hundred stayed behind, who were so faint that they couldn’t go over the brook Besor.
verses.arminianNotes:
Two hundred men are too faint to cross the brook, so David continues with four hundred. Arminian readers note that David does not shame the exhausted men but lets them stay.

Weakness is acknowledged without contempt.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see realistic leadership that accounts for human limits.

God’s victory will come through a reduced force, a pattern seen elsewhere in Scripture (cf. Judg 7:2–7).

verses.text: They found an Egyptian in the field, and brought him to David, and gave him bread, and he ate; and they gave him water to drink.
verses.arminianNotes:
They find an Egyptian in the field and give him bread and water. Arminian readers note the kindness shown to a stranger before his usefulness is known.

Compassion to the needy reflects God’s own care (cf. Lev 19:34).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also see mercy to a helpless man, which God then uses to guide David.

Kindness and providence meet. Both traditions see this as a picture of caring for the stranger (cf. Matt 25:35).

verses.text: They gave him a piece of a cake of figs and two clusters of raisins. When he had eaten, his spirit came again to him; for he had eaten no bread, and drank no water for three days and three nights.
verses.arminianNotes:
They give him figs and raisins, and his spirit returns; he had gone three days and nights without food or water. Arminian readers note the generous care that restores him.

The detail shows how near to death he was.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see God’s preservation of this man for his purpose.

The restoration of his strength makes possible the guidance he will give. Ordinary provision becomes the means of God’s plan.

verses.text: David asked him, “To whom do you belong? Where are you from?” He said, “I am a young man of Egypt, servant to an Amalekite; and my master left me, because three days ago I got sick.
verses.arminianNotes:
The Egyptian explains that he is servant to an Amalekite, abandoned three days earlier when he fell sick. Arminian readers note the cruelty of the master who left him.

The contrast between the Amalekite’s neglect and David’s men’s care is plain.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see how God uses the one cast aside by his master.

The abandoned servant becomes the key to the rescue, a reversal that fits the wider biblical pattern of God lifting up the lowly.

verses.text: We made a raid on the South of the Cherethites, and on that which belongs to Judah, and on the South of Caleb; and we burned Ziklag with fire.”
verses.arminianNotes:
He reports the raids on the South of the Cherethites, on Judah, and on the South of Caleb, and the burning of Ziklag. Arminian readers note that the raid covered a wide area.

The Cherethites are often associated with the Philistines, though their origins are discussed by interpreters.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see confirmation of who took Ziklag and where they went.

The mention of Judah and Caleb shows that David’s own people also suffered, which explains his later gifts to Judah’s elders (vv. 26–31).

verses.text: David said to him, “Will you bring me down to this troop?” He said, “Swear to me by God that you will not kill me and not deliver me up into the hands of my master, and I will bring you down to this troop.”
verses.arminianNotes:
David asks the Egyptian to lead him to the troop, and the Egyptian asks for an oath that David will not kill him or hand him back to his master. Arminian readers note that David’s protection of the vulnerable man is part of the agreement.

The oath is made “by God.”
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the seriousness of oaths before God and David’s willingness to protect a servant fleeing his master (cf. Deut 23:15–16).

The Egyptian’s request shows his fear, and David’s agreement shows mercy.

verses.text: When he had brought him down, behold, they were spread around over all the ground, eating, drinking, and dancing, because of all the great plunder that they had taken out of the land of the Philistines, and out of the land of Judah.
verses.arminianNotes:
The Egyptian brings David to the raiders, who are spread out eating, drinking, and dancing over their great plunder. Arminian readers note their careless celebration, unaware of danger.

The plunder came from both Philistine and Judean lands.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the false security of those who rejoice in wrongdoing.

The scene sets up the sudden reversal that God has promised David in verse 8.

verses.text: David struck them from the twilight even to the evening of the next day. Not a man of them escaped from there, except four hundred young men who rode on camels and fled.
verses.arminianNotes:
David attacks from twilight to the evening of the next day; only four hundred young men on camels escape. Arminian readers note the length and intensity of the battle.

The narrative reports the outcome briefly and without lingering on violence.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see God fulfilling his promise of victory.

The emphasis falls on the rescue, not on the fighting itself.

verses.text: David recovered all that the Amalekites had taken, and David rescued his two wives.
verses.arminianNotes:
“David recovered all that the Amalekites had taken, and David rescued his two wives.” Arminian readers note the fulfillment of God’s word in verse 8.

The repeated “all” stresses the completeness of the recovery.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see God’s promise kept exactly: “without fail recover all.”

David’s own household is restored along with everyone else’s. Both traditions see this as a testimony to God’s faithfulness.

verses.text: There was nothing lacking to them, neither small nor great, neither sons nor daughters, neither plunder, nor anything that they had taken. David brought them all back.
verses.arminianNotes:
Nothing was lacking, neither small nor great, sons nor daughters, nor plunder. Arminian readers note the joyful thoroughness of the restoration.

No family is left grieving.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see complete deliverance, echoing God’s earlier word.

The verse reverses verse 2 point by point, showing that God restores what was lost.

verses.text: David took all the flocks and the herds, which they drove before those other livestock, and said, “This is David’s plunder.”
verses.arminianNotes:
David takes the flocks and herds, and the people call it “David’s plunder.” Arminian readers note that the extra livestock taken from the Amalekites becomes David’s to distribute.

The wording of this verse is somewhat difficult, and translations vary.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see David’s growing honor among his followers.

How David uses this plunder in the following verses shows generosity rather than self-enrichment.
